messages.content: Can someone tell me what does “live learning steering delay” and “NNLC” do by having it on or off ?

(I'm also new to the model terminology, but this is how I understand it, so take my definitions with a grain of salt. Someone please correct me if I'm wrong)

"Live learning steering delay": Steering delay itself is how long it takes for the "model" to tell your car to turn (this includes the time it takes for the model to say "turn!" to your steering wheel turning and eventually to the car responding to the wheel being turned). Before, it used to be a static/constant number that was just set for each vehicle specifically (I think it's normally between 0.2 to 0.5 seconds). However, in the real world, it's almost never like that as everything has some variability. So they built something to actually just measure this delay for your car specifically instead of it being a set constant number. 

"Neural network lateral controller (NNLC)": I'm not sure if I can explain this too well in technical terms, but it's aim is to make the lateral control (your steering wheel moving) more human like and less jerky (though your mileage may vary based on your car). When your Comma driving model thinks it's off center and/or approaching a turn, it tells your steering wheel to move. Often times the torque controller is either moving too slowly and/or too hard (resulting in ping ponging, oversteering/understeering, and then it would have to correct itself), so NNLC was created to try and fix that. How it makes it more human like is magic to me and I have no idea how I would go about explaining it.
The description tells you for steer delay

My understanding is NNLC is about minimizing the gap between the commanded steering inputs (from the model) and what the car actually does.  That is, it applies one of five car-specific correction factor curves, by speed bands.   If the car wasn't steering so well with NNLC off *and you have a good model* then with it on, it can be smoother.   This can also go the other way, if the model is wonky.   Took me a while to figure out why with NNLC on the car started cutting lower-speed curves to the inside.  It was the model commanding it, and formerly the car just wasn't tracking to that model's (actually) problematic steering.   (The car was understeering.)  Switching to a better model - and leaving NNLC on, made it steer the best yet.

It is unclear if it wasn't trained properly the first time a few years ago, or if it drifted as the rest of the software changed. Signs of a model that needs retraining includes "weak torque at a particular speed/angle".

Perhaps you're referring to how it seems to smooth model jerkiness? That's a different part of NNLC. It looks ahead three planning intervals in the future. Then if the model's planner switches sign (flops wildly left and right) it can decide the model is not reliable right that moment so it has low confidence in using it. It also decides to not steer in situations where it won't overcome friction. The combination of these things seems to be dampening jerkiness of models. Some models are less jerky by design.

The other part that NNLC does is fine-tune the desired amount of torque needed at a particular speed and angle. No model is going to help this.
